title: Whiteflies
summary: Whiteflies are small sap-feeding insects whose eggs and immature stages occur primarily on leaf undersides. Adults may disperse when foliage is disturbed, while immature stages can be overlooked without deliberate inspection.
whatToLookFor: Tiny pale adults lifting from foliage when plants are disturbed
Eggs and flattened immature stages on leaf undersides
Localized chlorosis or reduced vigor under heavier pressure
Sticky honeydew or secondary sooty growth where populations are substantial
lookAlikes: Fungus gnat adults near the substrate
Small pale moths or other flying insects
Non-pest white residue on leaf undersides
General chlorosis from root-zone or nutritional stress
confirmWith: Inspect leaf undersides with magnification
Use sticky cards to monitor flying adults while still inspecting plants
Record life stages separately
Map hotspots rather than relying on whole-room presence or absence
managementPrinciples: Reduce movement from infested to clean zones
Remove heavily infested plant material when appropriate
Use life-stage-aware IPM and compatible biological controls where applicable
Re-scout after intervention to confirm population trend
prevention: Inspect incoming plants before release into production
Maintain weed and volunteer-plant sanitation
Use exclusion screening only with ventilation tradeoffs understood
Keep scouting records from the start of the crop

title: Root Aphids
summary: Root-feeding aphids can be difficult to detect because much of the population lives below the canopy. Declining vigor alone is not diagnostic; confirmation requires root-zone inspection and identification of the organism.
whatToLookFor: Small aphid-like insects on roots, container walls, or near drainage openings
Waxy residue or colonies in protected root-zone spaces
Winged forms appearing on monitoring cards during dispersal
Unexplained decline that coincides with confirmed root-zone insects
lookAlikes: Springtails and other harmless substrate arthropods
Low oxygen, salinity, or irrigation stress
confirmWith: Inspect representative roots and container edges under magnification
Collect specimens for reliable identification
Compare symptomatic and apparently healthy plants
Use sticky cards only as supplemental evidence for winged forms
managementPrinciples: Separate confirmed infested material
Avoid moving contaminated substrate or runoff between zones
Use an IPM plan matched to the identified pest and crop system
Track root-zone and aerial population signals over time
prevention: Quarantine incoming rooted material
Sanitize reusable containers and work areas
Avoid cross-zone runoff
Maintain lot identity for propagation material

title: Mealybugs & Scale Insects
summary: Mealybugs and scale insects can hide at nodes, petioles, stems, and protected crevices. Their waxy coverings and low mobility in some life stages make deliberate close inspection important.
whatToLookFor: Cottony or waxy colonies in protected plant crevices
Small fixed or slow-moving scale-like bodies on stems or leaves
Honeydew and sticky surfaces
Localized decline around persistent colonies
confirmWith: Inspect with magnification and a probe to distinguish organisms from residue
Look for multiple life stages
Check nodes, petiole bases, and sheltered branch unions
Photograph and preserve specimens if identification is uncertain
managementPrinciples: Detect early before colonies establish in inaccessible areas
Physically separate infested material
Use compatible biological or other IPM tactics appropriate to the pest
Verify control by checking hidden sites, not only exposed foliage
prevention: Inspect incoming vegetative material closely
Clean propagation and mother-stock areas
Avoid carrying insects on tools, clothing, or plant carts
Remove abandoned plant material that can serve as a reservoir

title: Leafhoppers & Other Mobile Sap Feeders
summary: Mobile sap-feeding insects can create stippling, chlorosis, distortion, or localized feeding marks, but damage pattern alone rarely identifies the insect responsible.
whatToLookFor: Small wedge-shaped insects that move quickly or jump
Feeding injury on leaves
Cast skins or insects along veins and leaf undersides
Hotspots near entry points in protected structures or field edges outdoors
confirmWith: Observe the insect directly
Use sweep, tap, or sticky-card monitoring where appropriate
Inspect fresh injury rather than old damaged leaves alone
Record insect abundance with symptom progression
managementPrinciples: Identify the insect before selecting a tactic
Limit entry and movement where practical
Use scouting to determine whether pressure is increasing or transient
Consider vector risk only when a relevant pathogen and vector relationship is established
prevention: Maintain exclusion and sanitation around openings
Control volunteer host plants where appropriate
Inspect outdoor edges and greenhouse vents
Keep monitoring records

title: Caterpillars & Chewing Insects
summary: Chewing insects remove tissue rather than extracting sap. Holes, missing leaf margins, frass, webbing, and direct sightings are stronger evidence than general discoloration.
whatToLookFor: Irregular holes or missing leaf tissue
Frass on leaves or inside flower clusters
Larvae, webbing, or feeding shelters
Localized flower injury that can create secondary disease opportunities
confirmWith: Inspect the plant at multiple times of day
Open folded leaves or webbed areas carefully
Look for frass and larvae together
Identify larvae before choosing management
managementPrinciples: Remove or isolate heavily infested material where practical
Use stage-specific biological or other IPM tactics
Inspect flower interiors because hidden feeding can be missed
Re-scout for eggs and small larvae after larger larvae are removed
prevention: Screen protected structures appropriately
Inspect outdoor plants after moth activity or new feeding
Remove nearby plant debris that shelters pests where relevant
Maintain regular whole-plant scouting

title: Beneficial Arthropods & Biological Control
summary: Predators and parasitoids can be valuable IPM tools, but success depends on matching the beneficial organism to the pest and life stage, releasing it under suitable conditions, and verifying performance through scouting.
whatToLookFor: Predatory mites or insects on plants and monitoring surfaces
Parasitized pest stages where applicable
Changes in pest population trend after release
Environmental conditions that affect beneficial establishment
lookAlikes: Pest mites mistaken for predatory mites
Empty pest skins interpreted as parasitism without confirmation
Short-term pest decline unrelated to the release
confirmWith: Identify beneficial and pest organisms separately
Record release date, rate, and location
Scout repeatedly after release
Review pesticide compatibility before and after release
managementPrinciples: Use biological control as part of an IPM program rather than a one-time rescue
Start early when the selected beneficial strategy depends on establishment
Protect beneficial populations from incompatible broad-spectrum treatments
Judge success by population trends and crop condition
prevention: Build scouting into routine crop work
Train staff to distinguish beneficials from pests
Maintain supplier and release records
Design greenhouse zones so hotspots can be treated without disrupting the entire program

title: Fusarium-Associated Wilt & Crown Disease
summary: Fusarium species can be associated with root, crown, and vascular disease, but wilt and vascular discoloration are not specific enough for diagnosis by appearance alone.
whatToLookFor: Progressive wilt not fully explained by short-term water status
Root or crown discoloration
Stem or vascular discoloration in affected tissue
Uneven decline among plants sharing similar above-canopy conditions
lookAlikes: Severe drought or low root oxygen
confirmWith: Inspect roots, crown, and vascular tissue together
Submit representative symptomatic tissue to a diagnostic laboratory when confirmation matters
Compare irrigation and root-zone records
Avoid assigning species from color alone
managementPrinciples: Separate diseased material from healthy propagation stock
Correct water-management conditions that favor root decline
Sanitize tools, surfaces, and reusable containers
Use confirmed diagnosis to guide crop-removal and prevention decisions
prevention: Start with clean propagation material
Prevent contaminated water or debris movement
Avoid chronic saturation and root injury
Maintain lot records for mother and clone material
visualNeeds: Fusarium-associated disease versus abiotic wilt comparison

title: Pythium-Associated Root Rot
summary: Pythium-associated root disease is favored by vulnerable roots and water-mediated spread in many production systems. Brown roots or wilt alone are not enough to establish the cause.
whatToLookFor: Loss of healthy fine-root structure
Root discoloration and tissue sloughing in advanced cases
Wilt or reduced vigor despite adequate bulk moisture
Patterns associated with shared irrigation or chronically wet zones
confirmWith: Inspect root tissue and root-zone conditions
Compare affected and unaffected irrigation zones
Use laboratory diagnosis for important outbreaks
Review water movement and sanitation history
managementPrinciples: Reduce conditions that chronically deprive roots of oxygen
Prevent contaminated water from recirculating without appropriate treatment
Remove severely affected plants when they become inoculum reservoirs
Clean and disinfect appropriate equipment between crops
prevention: Maintain good drainage and irrigation control
Use clean propagation material and media
Keep floors and drains clean
Monitor roots before canopy symptoms become severe
visualNeeds: Pythium versus abiotic root stress comparison

title: Leaf Spot Disease Complexes
summary: Leaf spots and lesions can be produced by fungal, bacterial, environmental, chemical, and physical causes. Pattern, progression, environmental context, and laboratory evidence are often needed to separate them.
whatToLookFor: Lesion shape, margin, color, and tissue age
Whether spots cross veins or follow splash patterns
New lesions appearing after wet periods
Visible sporulation or structures under magnification when present
confirmWith: Track lesion progression over time
Inspect both leaf surfaces with magnification
Review recent sprays and environmental wetness
Use diagnostic testing when the outbreak is important or unusual
managementPrinciples: Avoid assuming every spot is a deficiency
Reduce unnecessary leaf wetness and splash where relevant
Remove heavily diseased tissue when appropriate
Use confirmed diagnosis to choose further action
prevention: Maintain sanitation and airflow
Avoid moving contaminated splash water
Inspect incoming material
Record foliar applications and environmental events

title: Virus Disease & Vector Concepts
summary: Plant viruses can cause mottling, distortion, stunting, or no obvious symptoms. Diagnosis requires testing because similar patterns can come from nutrition, herbicide or spray injury, mites, temperature stress, or genetic variation.
whatToLookFor: Persistent mottling or mosaic-like color patterns
Distorted or reduced new growth
Symptoms repeating in clonally related plants
Patterns associated with a known vector or contaminated propagation chain when relevant
confirmWith: Use validated laboratory testing for the suspected pathogen
Record plant lineage and propagation source
Identify any suspected vector rather than assuming transmission
Compare symptoms across clonally related material
managementPrinciples: Do not propagate confirmed infected stock
Separate suspect material while testing
Control established vectors when a verified vector relationship exists
Sanitize propagation practices to limit mechanical or stock-mediated spread where relevant
prevention: Use clean tested mother stock when available
Quarantine incoming clones
Maintain propagation records
Train staff not to diagnose viruses visually

title: Bacterial Disease Concepts
summary: Bacterial plant diseases can produce water-soaked lesions, blights, rots, or vascular symptoms depending on the organism and tissue involved, but those signs overlap with fungal disease and abiotic injury.
whatToLookFor: Water-soaked or rapidly expanding lesions
Tissue collapse or soft decay in susceptible zones
Patterns associated with splash or wounds
Repeated symptoms following contaminated tools or propagation events
confirmWith: Submit representative tissue for laboratory diagnosis when confirmation matters
Document recent pruning, propagation, splash, and sanitation history
Compare progression under dry versus wet conditions
Inspect for mixed infections
managementPrinciples: Separate affected material
Reduce avoidable splash and wounding
Sanitize tools and surfaces appropriately
Use diagnosis-specific management rather than generic antimicrobial assumptions
prevention: Clean propagation workflow
Avoid reusing contaminated water or tools
Inspect incoming stock
Keep detailed lot and sanitation records

title: Post-Harvest Mold & Microbial Risk
summary: Harvested flowers remain biologically active and can support microbial growth when moisture availability, temperature, contaminated material, and handling conditions align. Visible mold is a rejection signal, not a quality defect to blend away.
whatToLookFor: Visible fungal growth or unusual powdery/fuzzy colonies
Soft, discolored, or collapsing flower tissue
Musty or otherwise abnormal odor
Localized moisture or condensation inside storage containers
confirmWith: Use magnification to distinguish trichomes from fungal structures
Separate suspect material from clean lots
Review drying and water-activity records
Use laboratory testing where product safety or compliance requires it
managementPrinciples: Do not mix visibly moldy material into clean product
Correct drying and storage conditions
Clean contact surfaces and containers
Investigate the environmental or handling source rather than only removing one affected flower
prevention: Harvest sanitation
Representative drying measurements
Validated water-activity or moisture-control practices
Clean dry storage with appropriate packaging
